title: Transaction
text: My father, who had been deep in thought, looked up and spoke.
“How much would it cost to buy a Filolial directly?”
“…Starting at 200 coins for an adult, I suppose. It depends on the plumage and breed. Yes.”
“If an adult costs that much, does that mean chicks are cheaper? And if we’re just talking about the price of the egg—excluding the cost of raising it—is it a good deal?”
“No, no—the eggs over there are all the same.”
“I see… That’s why you called it a lottery. What’s the price of a flying dragon?”
“At market rates, hitting the jackpot is equivalent to 20 gold coins.”
“By the way, what are the odds? Just for the ones that yield that dragon’s egg.”
“We’ve prepared 250 eggs for this lottery. It’s one out of those 250.”
My father fell deep into thought. One in 250… Those odds are pretty steep. Well, we don’t really need a dragon anyway.
“We’ve cast powerful Magic so you can’t tell by appearance or weight. You must agree to the possibility of drawing a blank before making a purchase.”
“You’re running a good business.”
“Yes. We ask winners to provide their names and have them participate in our advertising.”
“Hmm, the odds are…”
“If you buy ten, you can choose one from this box, which is guaranteed to contain a prize. Here you go.”
“It’s kind of like one of those pay-to-win games… I’m sure it doesn’t actually contain a ‘Dragon Rider’ or anything like that, does it?”
“No. However, you’re guaranteed to win something worth 300 silver coins.”
My father slumped his shoulders in disappointment. He muttered under his breath, “Gacha.”
“Hmm…”
Then he turned to look at me.
“Motoyasu, come here for a moment.”
My Father beckoned me over.
“What is it?”
“You might not know this, Motoyasu, but I think the future me probably tried his luck at this egg lottery here. I’m guessing there’s a high chance I won a girl named Filo there.”
“Why is that?”
Instead of choosing Filo-tan… why would he choose something that might be a dud? I just can’t understand it at all.

“Even if it were a dud, this is a trading post run by monster merchants. I’m absolutely certain I would’ve thought, ‘Even if the monster’s useless, I can just raise it and sell it.’ Keel-kun’s price just skyrocketed a moment ago, but if I had a slave with me for the same reason—and especially right after being told the same thing—it would make even more sense.”
My father paused for a moment before pointing at the lottery again.
“So you’re taking a chance on something cheap—yet with a chance to boost your combat strength… If I were in your shoes, with no capital and only one ally, I might very well do the same.”

I see. So you’re saying there’s a high probability that my Father acquired Filo-tan through the lottery. That was a blind spot for me. Perhaps the Monster Merchant didn’t count Filolial-sama, who was mixed in with the monster lottery tickets, as part of the total.
“Hmm… Well then, instead of the 100 silver coins as the entry fee, I’ll pay 200—so exclude everything except Filolial and the dragon.”
“That… even a Hero like you couldn’t possibly agree to that. Yes.”
“…Hmm, then let’s make a deal right here.”
“Meaning…?”
My Father whispered something to the Monster Merchant. Then he pointed at Sakura-chan.
“Sakura, transform into a monster.”
“Eh? Sakura, I don’t really want to do that right here… Oh, but since Naofumi called me by my first name, I’ll do my best.”
With a puff, Sakura-chan transformed into the Filolial Queen. Just that alone made the Monster Merchant’s eyes widen in astonishment.

“So there you have it. What do you say? For 100 silver coins, would you mind limiting your selection to just Filolial and dragon eggs? The Filolial or dragons hatched from those eggs will come here regularly to report. Whether you value this information as cheap or expensive… which side are you on?”
The Monster Merchant thought for a moment, then nodded.
“Understood. In that case, I’ll exclude all eggs other than those containing Filolials and flying dragons. Yes!”
“Sakura, that’s enough.”
“Okay!”

Sakura-chan returned to her angelic form. Just as I’d expect from my Father. Since he couldn’t get his way with money, he sold information to force the issue. That’s a tactic I never would’ve thought of. The eggs inside the monster lottery were being removed one after another.
“So, this is the lottery containing only Filolial and Dragon eggs. Here you go.”

With the lottery now riddled with holes, my Father beckoned me over. He wants me to find out if Filo-tan is in here. But I don’t remember the scent of Filo-tan when she was a hatchling. Still, I’ll narrow it down based on the scents I’ve smelled so far.

From what I can tell, it seems the eggs I bought last time are mixed in here as well. After sorting through them, a few eggs emerged. I pointed at them subtly, and after some hesitation, my Father chose one.

“Isn’t that all of them?” I asked. When I looked at him, he shook his head. Then, in a low voice, he said, “It’d be tough to handle if they multiplied too much under the current circumstances.” Well, procuring food every day is a struggle, after all.
“Understood. I, Motoyasu, will exercise restraint.”
“Then I’ll take this one. As for the rest—this and this… set these aside for me; I’ll buy them later.”
“Understood. Yes, sir.”

That wraps up the reservation. As expected of my Father—he leaves nothing to chance. There’s a clear difference in skill compared to someone like me, who bought up everything but still couldn’t get my hands on Filo-tan. Indeed, if he’s having them set aside, the chances of someone else snatching Filo-tan away are drastically reduced.
“Since you already own a Filolial, I assume you understand the contract terms. Yes.”
“Ah.”
Father places the egg into the incubator prepared by the Monster Merchant and takes it.
“If it doesn’t hatch, I’ll come back and demand a penalty fee or something.”
“Even if you end up with a dud, you won’t go down without a fight—I take my hat off to you, a hero who’s such a skilled negotiator!”

It seems the Monster Merchant really takes a liking to my Father. His energy level is clearly different from when he was dealing with me. However, my Father, Keel, Sakura-chan, and I can all tell he’s nearing his limit. His gait seems a bit unsteady, after all.
“Even if it’s just a verbal agreement, I’ll really be coming. If you try to back out, my slave—the Spear Hero—will go on a rampage.”
“A hero as a slave? Can’t you make a hero a slave?”
“Is that so? Hmph… Being bound by Magic isn’t the only way to make someone a slave. I’ve made sure this guy will do anything I say. Right?”
“That’s right. If it’s Father’s command, I’ll turn this place into ruins right this very moment.”
If it’s Father’s command, I, Motoyasu, will steal Filolial-sama’s egg and then turn this tent into a pile of ashes.
“I see, I see! Even the Hero is a slave—the Shield Hero’s skill far exceeds my imagination. Yes.”
My Father handed the monster merchant 100 silver coins. And so, we ended up purchasing a new egg that appears to belong to Filolial-sama.
“Phew… I still can’t get used to it. That guy… he’s a decent businessman to deal with, but I don’t want to get too close to him.”
“Bro, how do you even deal with that guy?”
“He’s not a difficult person, but… it’s like… the more you get to know him, the more you feel like he’ll drag you into some deep, dark place. He’s kind of scary.”
“Is that so? When I dealt with him, he seemed to keep a strange distance.”
“Well… it’s Motoyasu-kun, isn’t it?”
My Father is nodding with an expression that suggests he’s understood something. What does that mean, I wonder?
“He’s kind, but he gives off a chill, doesn’t he!”
“That’s exactly the right feeling.”
“Hmm… there is a bad vibe.”
So Sakura-chan felt it too. However, according to my future Father, it’s definitely a reputable shop. Well, there are other good shops to buy Filolial-sama from, of course.
“Now that you mention it, you’re right… That person’s vibe is different from other merchants who are blatantly malicious.”
“Is that so? I’ve never been a slave, so I don’t really know.”

My future Father asked this in response to Keel’s remark. A slave trader, you say? I did hear a long time ago—back when I was trying to help my Big Sister—that such professions exist in this country. After my Big Sister scolded me, I did a bit of research myself.

In the country of Melromarc, there’s a practice of enslaving Demi-Humans. I’ve actually visited a few other shops besides that monster merchant’s. ……How should I put it? I do believe there’s a definite difference in how that monster merchant and other slave traders treat their slaves.

“Before my brother bought me, there was a place where—even though we were both Demi-Humans—some guy actually whipped me! I don’t know if I was his favorite or just a leftover, but he beat me with a smile on his face because the slave trader ordered him to.”
“Ugh…”

The slaves at the monster merchant’s place may lack a fighting spirit, but I don’t get the sense that they’re subjected to public floggings or similar acts inside the shop as a spectacle. He has several burly, strong men working for him, whereas at other slave merchants, Demi-Human slaves often fill that role. Perhaps there’s a certain sense of restraint in that regard.
“So it wasn’t at that slave trader’s place.”

“Then maybe that slave trader is trying to prevent the establishment of hierarchical relationships among the slaves themselves? Or maybe he understood that abuse is strictly something the customers do…”
“He’s not a good person, but he’s a creepy guy—I can’t even tell if he’s a bad person or not.”
“I won’t deny that.”
And with that, my conversation with my father and Keel came to an end.
